newsitem.title: Netherlands: Head of EU's Albania team has UN, OSCE background.
newsitem.headline: Head of EU's Albania team has UN, OSCE background.

text.p: Count Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg, who heads the European Union's high-level mission to Albania, is a career diplomat with some experience of dealing with the Balkans.
The Dutch aristocrat was arriving in Tirana on Monday with a team of Dutch, Greek and Italian diplomats for his second visit in two weeks.

De Marchant, 55, who was previously deputy head of the Netherlands' mission to the United Nations in New York, was involved in the diplomatic fallout of the alleged Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia in July, 1995.
He tried to persuade the United Nations to investigate the alleged massacre by Bosnian Serbs of several thousand captured Moslems, on behalf of the Dutch government.
De Marchant failed, and in a report to Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo he concluded that there was little appetite within the U.N. for a full-blown investigation.
The Bosnian Serbs say the allegations are exaggerated and distorted.
But Srebrenica remains imprinted on the Dutch consciousness because of the role of Dutch U.N. peacekeeping troops, who failed to stop the killing.
And it underlines the difficulties of Western involvement in the Balkans.
European Union foreign ministers have shied away from sending troops to Albania, deciding instead to offer military and police expertise in a strictly advisory capacity.
De Marchant's mission is to discuss how these experts can help restore order in the anarchic Balkan state.
"It is not a fact-finding mission...more a mission to establish what concrete needs there are and how we can help to meet them," he told Dutch radio before departing.
During his previous visit, De Marchant met President Sali Berisha and then prime minister Aleksander Meksi who has since resigned.

He also accompanied Franz Vranitzky of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) who met Albanian government and rebel leaders on board an Italian frigate in the Adriatic Sea last Friday.
The Dutch foreign ministry said De Marchant had spent his entire career in the diplomatic service where he currently holds the post of roving ambassador for special missions.
From 1986 to 1989 he was part of his country's delegation to the conference which led to the creation of OSCE.

After a brief spell back in the Netherlands, he served at the Dutch mission to the United Nations from 1990 to 1994, returning to The Hague to head the foreign ministry section responsible for bilateral ties with other European countries.

De Marchant said he expected the team to remain in Albania until Wednesday or Thursday, adding that he would present his report to EU foreign ministers as soon as possible and in any case before the ministers' next meeting on March 24.
